aliases.name: Curupira
aliases.meaning: Closely related Tupi-Guarani forest spirit, sometimes equated with the Chullachaqui

aliases.name: Shapingo
aliases.meaning: Local variant name in mestizo folklore

description.summary: The Chullachaqui (Quechua chulla 'odd / unequal' + chaki 'foot') is a forest spirit of Peruvian and Brazilian Amazonia, depicted as a small humanoid with one mismatched foot — typically one human foot and one animal hoof — who shapeshifts into a familiar person to lead unwary travellers astray.
description.full: The Chullachaqui (also spelled Chullachaki, Shapingo, or in Brazilian Portuguese Curupira) is one of the most widespread forest spirits of the Western Amazon basin, attested in Quechua, Cocama-Cocamilla, Shipibo-Conibo, Yagua, and mestizo riverine traditions of Peru, eastern Ecuador, and adjoining Brazilian Amazonia. The figure is consistently described as a small (roughly one-metre) male humanoid with one foot conspicuously different from the other — usually one human foot and one animal foot (a deer, peccary, jaguar, tapir, or rooster), in some versions reversed or twisted. The Chullachaqui's central narrative function is shapeshifting: it appears in the form of a relative, friend, or trusted local in order to lure a victim deep into the forest, then reveals its true nature and leaves the person hopelessly disoriented, sometimes for days. The mismatched foot is the only sure way to detect the deception, since the spirit cannot disguise its footprints. Beyond pranks, the Chullachaqui is widely understood as a guardian (dueño) of the forest, its plants, and its game animals; respectful behaviour, ritual offerings (typically of mapacho tobacco) and an apology before hunting are traditional means of avoiding its anger. Modern Amazonian shamanism, particularly the ayahuasca traditions of Loreto and Ucayali, integrates the Chullachaqui into its cosmology as a powerful but dangerous spirit teacher; eco-tourism and contemporary literature have also adopted it as a symbol of Amazonian conservation.

etymology.meaning: 'One foot' or 'mismatched foot', referring to its diagnostic feature.
etymology.first_use: Quechua oral tradition predates documented written usage; recorded in Spanish-language Amazonian ethnographic and folkloric collections from the 19th and 20th centuries onward.

related_phenomena.name: Curupira
related_phenomena.description: Brazilian (Tupi-Guarani) forest spirit with backward-pointing feet; closely cognate with the Chullachaqui

related_phenomena.name: Duende
related_phenomena.description: Spanish-American small forest/household spirit; shares trickster forest-guardian role

related_phenomena.name: Patasola
related_phenomena.description: Colombian one-legged forest spirit who lures men deep into the forest

related_phenomena.name: La Tunda
related_phenomena.description: Afro-Colombian forest spirit who shape-shifts into loved ones to lure victims

related_phenomena.name: El Sisimite
related_phenomena.description: Central American forest spirit / hairy hominid in shared 'forest abductor' tradition

related_phenomena.name: Yacuruna
related_phenomena.description: Aquatic counterpart in Amazonian cosmology; underwater spirits whose terrestrial complement includes the Chullachaqui

features.description: One human foot and one animal foot (deer, peccary, jaguar, tapir, or rooster) — diagnostic feature visible in tracks
Often wears a large straw hat that conceals its face

features.feature: Wrinkled face / large nose / pointed ears
features.description: When seen unmasked, has an elderly face with red eyes
Wears ragged, dirty clothes, sometimes the remains of indigenous or mestizo dress
Walks hunched over with a noticeably limping step

physical.morphology: Humanoid, dwarf-stature, with one diagnostic non-human foot; otherwise resembles a poorly dressed elderly indigenous or mestizo man.

abilities.description: Takes the form of a known relative, friend, or familiar villager to mislead the victim
Imitates the voice of loved ones to call victims deeper into the forest
Causes travellers to lose their way, walk in circles, and fail to find familiar landmarks
Said to govern movements of game animals; angering it makes hunts unsuccessful
In some versions, challenges victims to a fight or wager for hidden treasures

habitat_preference: Ceiba and lupuna trees (especially Chullachaqui caspi, Brysonima crassifolia, identified locally as its tree)
behavior.diet: Said to feed on game and forest fruits as a forest dweller; occasionally tobacco offerings
patterns: Approaches solitary travellers, often hunters and woodcutters
Manifests in forms most likely to be trusted by the specific victim
Most actively associated with hunters who have broken taboos (over-hunting, taking pregnant females, leaving carcasses to spoil)
Encounters often occur in the deep forest away from established paths

range.description: Western Amazon basin: lowland Peru (especially Loreto, Ucayali, San Martín, and Madre de Dios), eastern Ecuador (Pastaza, Napo), western Brazil (Acre, Amazonas), and the headwaters region of Colombia and Bolivia.

hotspots.name: Iquitos and surrounding rainforest

location.description: Capital of the Peruvian department of Loreto; centre of mestizo and indigenous Amazonian folklore

hotspots.notes: Chullachaqui is a defining figure of riverine and rainforest folklore around Iquitos and is invoked in shamanic and ecotourism contexts.

hotspots.name: Pucallpa / Ucayali River

location.description: Ucayali river port; centre of Shipibo-Conibo culture

hotspots.notes: Chullachaqui (Shipibo: a related figure) features in Shipibo-Conibo oral tradition and ayahuasca cosmology.

first_recorded.source: Quechua and adjoining Amazonian oral traditions; first written attestations in Spanish-language ethnographic literature of the 19th–20th centuries

peak_activity_periods.description: Documentation by Peruvian folklorists and indigenous-language linguists
Renewed prominence through Amazonian ecotourism, ayahuasca tourism, and conservation discourse

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Most strongly associated with the dry season, when hunters and woodcutters travel further into the forest and encounters are most reported.

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Columbian Quechua-speaking Andean and Amazonian populations almost certainly maintained 'forest owner' (dueño del monte) traditions of which the Chullachaqui is a regional expression. Cognate figures in the Tupi-Guarani Curupira and in Andean apus and aukis suggest a deep South American substrate of forest-guardian beings.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest written documentation occurs in 19th- and 20th-century Spanish-language ethnographies and folkloric collections of the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon; the figure is treated as already long-established in oral tradition.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely related to the Brazilian Curupira (with reversed feet), Colombian Patasola (one-legged forest woman), and Central American sisimites; part of a continental class of 'forest-guardian / disorientation spirit' figures.

timeline.event: Quechua and Amazonian oral traditions of forest-owning spirits include the chulla-chaki figure
Spanish chroniclers in the Andes and Amazon record duendes and forest-spirit traditions among indigenous peoples
timeline.significance: Provides earliest colonial-period framing of Amazonian forest-spirit beliefs (general; the Chullachaqui by name is later)

timeline.event: Peruvian folklorists (e.g. Mario Florián, Arturo Jiménez Borja) and indigenous-language scholars publish accounts of Chullachaqui in collections of Amazonian myth and legend
timeline.significance: Anchors the figure in academic folklore studies

timeline.event: Chullachaqui becomes a routine subject in Amazonian shamanic and ayahuasca-tourism literature, including works by Luis Eduardo Luna and Steve Beyer
timeline.significance: Brings the figure into wider international awareness
timeline.source: Luna, L. E. & Amaringo, P. (1991), Ayahuasca Visions; Beyer, S. (2009), Singing to the Plants

history.modern_era: The Chullachaqui retains a vivid presence in contemporary Amazonian life: it appears in school curricula in Peruvian Amazonian regions, in mestizo and indigenous storytelling, in conservation campaigns, in mural and street art in Iquitos and Pucallpa, and in films, novels, and graphic works. Within Amazonian shamanism, the term Chullachaqui is also used for an apprentice's spirit-teacher or for a phantasmal double encountered in plant-medicine work.

documentary.name: Pablo Amaringo's Ayahuasca Visions (1991)
documentary.description: Numerous paintings by Peruvian shaman-artist Pablo Amaringo, published with anthropologist Luis Eduardo Luna, depict the Chullachaqui as encountered in ayahuasca visions. The works are widely cited as a primary source for modern Amazonian iconography of the spirit.
documentary.analysis: While not 'evidence' of the spirit's reality, the corpus is a documentary record of how the Chullachaqui is visualised in contemporary Amazonian shamanism.
documentary.source: Luna, L. E. & Amaringo, P. (1991), Ayahuasca Visions: The Religious Iconography of a Peruvian Shaman

paranormal.name: Forest-owner (dueño) cosmology
paranormal.description: Indigenous Amazonian cosmologies hold that each tract of forest, river, or species has a non-human owner that must be respected. The Chullachaqui is the western Amazonian expression of this principle in human form.
proponents: Indigenous knowledge holders of the Western Amazon
evidence_cited: Continuity of dueño beliefs across South American indigenous societies
Ritual practice of asking permission and offering tobacco before hunting

skeptical.name: Cultural framework for forest disorientation
skeptical.description: Sceptics argue the Chullachaqui narrative is an explanatory device for the genuine and well-documented psychological phenomenon of becoming lost in dense rainforest, where direction-finding is difficult and panic distorts memory.
evidence_cited: Psychological literature on getting lost (e.g., Hill, K. 1998)
Cross-cultural pattern of 'forest abduction' explanatory tales

skeptical.name: Educational and ecological function
skeptical.description: Folklorists argue the Chullachaqui story functions as a culturally embedded conservation ethic, encoding norms about not over-hunting, not wasting carcasses, and respecting forest taboos.
evidence_cited: Ethnographic evidence that hunters who break specific taboos are said to be especially vulnerable
Use of the Chullachaqui in modern Amazonian environmental education

traditions: Quechua oral tradition of the Andean foothills and Western Amazon
Cocama-Cocamilla, Shipibo-Conibo, Yagua, Kichwa, and Asháninka oral traditions
Mestizo riverine folklore of the Peruvian Amazon
Brazilian Caboclo folklore overlapping with Curupira
stories: The hunter who follows his 'cousin' into the forest and is lost for days
The woodcutter who recognises the Chullachaqui by its mismatched footprint and escapes
The wager-and-fight motif in which the Chullachaqui offers hidden treasure
folklore.beliefs: The Chullachaqui is a real being that should be neither sought nor mocked. Hunters and travellers offer mapacho tobacco and ask permission before entering deep forest, and avoid speaking its name unnecessarily.

indigenous.significance: Integrates ecological, spiritual, and ethical knowledge: the Chullachaqui enforces respectful conduct in the forest, polices over-hunting, and represents the boundary between human and non-human worlds.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: The Chullachaqui is a living tradition for many indigenous and mestizo Amazonian communities; popular accounts should not flatten it into a 'cute' or generic forest spirit. Distinct local versions exist in different languages.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite indigenous interlocutors and local Spanish- or Portuguese-language sources directly. Avoid commercialising or trivialising the figure in connection with ayahuasca tourism.
